edits.old: The check uses one receiver's $A_{\rm mode}$, so it assumes that all 50 photoelectrons, and all four of Waymo's speckles, arrive through one receiver. With four separate receivers, as in the §C7a design, the same 50 photoelectrons would need $1.35/4\approx0.34$ µJ, below Waymo's range, so the agreement holds only if Waymo's four speckles come from within one receiver.
edits.new: One receiver is the right basis for the check, because Waymo takes all four speckles through one single-mode receiver: it sums the FFT spectra of successive acquisitions, between which the scanning beam has moved enough to decorrelate the speckle, and its 50 is the total over the four acquisitions [P, Piggott et al. 2025, §3.2 and Fig. 8(b)]. The §C7a design takes its four looks through four receivers at once instead, which divides the energy for the same 50 photoelectrons by four, to $1.35/4\approx0.34$ µJ.
edits.why: Source found by the R4_C7-C7b_F6 research agent; see sources/R4_C7-C7b_F6_findings.md, R4_C7-C7b_F6-01.

edits.old: Eq. (93) for one receiver with $A_{\rm mode}=74.5$ mm² (a 20 mm aperture at 250 m) and $\eta=0.25$ gives $50\times1.28\times10^{-19}\times\pi\times250^2/(0.05\times7.45\times10^{-5}\times0.25)=1.35$ µJ, inside that range.
edits.new: Eq. (93) for one receiver with $A_{\rm mode}=74.5$ mm² (a 20 mm aperture at 250 m) and $\eta=0.25$ gives $50\times1.28\times10^{-19}\times\pi\times250^2/(0.05\times7.45\times10^{-5}\times0.25)=1.35$ µJ for one ramp. Waymo's energy per point pays for two chirps of 50 photons each: its ideal 0.52 µJ is $2\times50\times1.28\times10^{-19}\ {\rm J}/(2.45\times10^{-11})$, through a −106.1 dB worst-case link [P, Piggott et al. 2025, Table 1]. The like-for-like value is therefore $2\times1.35=2.7$ µJ at $\eta=0.25$, 1.6–3.3× Waymo's range, or 1.35 µJ at $\eta=0.5$, the efficiency of Waymo's 3 dB case, which lies inside it [E].
edits.why: Source found by the R4_C7-C7b_F6 research agent; see sources/R4_C7-C7b_F6_findings.md, R4_C7-C7b_F6-01.

edits.old: Integrated alternatives are SiN self-injection-locked lasers (42 kHz, 0.65% nonlinearity) and thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) E-DBR lasers (378 kHz, 1.5%) [P, Bianconi et al. 2025]. Read as peak frequency deviations over a 1 GHz sweep, the reading applied to Waymo's figure above, those nonlinearities are 6.5 and 15 MHz, ≈100–240× the 62.5 kHz that Eq. (108) allows at 300 m. Read as fractional chirp-rate errors, they are still 13–30× above the $5\times10^{-4}$ that 15 cm at 300 m tolerates. Either way they need pre-distortion or resampling [E].
edits.new:
Integrated alternatives are SiN self-injection-locked lasers (42 kHz linewidth over 1 ms, 0.65% nonlinearity) and TFLN E-DBR lasers (378 kHz over 1 ms, 1.5%) [I, Bianconi et al. 2025]. Bianconi et al. define the nonlinearity $\sigma$ as the RMS deviation of the laser frequency from a least-squares straight ramp, divided by the sweep excursion $B$ [I, Bianconi et al. 2025, Supplementary Eq. (4)]. The 0.65% belongs to an unpackaged self-injection-locked chip swept over 500 MHz, which reached 0.08% over 210 MHz once packaged [I, Voloshin et al. 2025]; the 1.5% was measured over a 10.5 GHz sweep [I, Siddharth et al. 2025]. For the parabolic bow of Eq. (108) the peak deviation from the chord is $3\sqrt5/2\approx3.35$ times the RMS deviation, so $\delta
u_{\max}=3.35\,\sigma B$ and $\varepsilon=8\delta
u_{\max}/B=12\sqrt5\,\sigma\approx27\sigma$. If the same fractions hold over a 1 GHz sweep, 0.65% and 1.5% give $\delta
u_{\max}\approx22$ and 50 MHz, or $\varepsilon\approx0.17$ and 0.40: about 350× and 800× the 62.5 kHz (equivalently the $5	imes10^{-4}$) that Eq. (108) allows for 15 cm at 300 m. The packaged 0.08% is still about 43× too large. They need pre-distortion or resampling [E].

edits.old: Commercial distributed-feedback lasers (DFBs) reach tens of kHz. At 300 m the SiN self-injection-locked laser below (42 kHz) loses 2.3 dB and the TFLN E-DBR laser (378 kHz) 21 dB [E].
edits.new: Narrow-linewidth grades of commercial distributed-feedback lasers (DFBs) reach tens of kHz: AeroDIODE specifies its 20 mW and 40 mW 1550 nm butterfly DFBs at <50 kHz, measured by the phase-noise method at 1 MHz [P, AeroDIODE datasheets PN_A75 and PN_A79, 2026], and Waymo notes that several vendors offer DFBs with linewidths in the low tens of kHz [P, Piggott et al. 2025]. A standard commercial DFB measured by Bianconi et al. showed 802 kHz over 1 ms [I]. The integrated lasers below are quoted with linewidths over 1 ms, which slow frequency noise dominates. The SiN self-injection-locked laser (42 kHz over 1 ms) has a 3 Hz intrinsic linewidth [I, Voloshin et al. 2025], and the TFLN extended distributed Bragg reflector (E-DBR) laser (378 kHz over 1 ms) one of 2.8 kHz [I, Siddharth et al. 2025]. Taken as Lorentzian widths in Eq. (110), the 1 ms values would cost 2.3 dB and 21 dB at 300 m, but the lasers' measured frequency-noise spectra in Eq. (109) give less than 0.01 dB and about 0.2–0.4 dB (up to ≈0.9 dB for a 16 µs useful window) [E].

edits.new: Aurora ran 10 driverless trucks in December 2025 and reduced that fleet in early 2026 to prepare a second-generation fleet [P, Q4 2025 shareholder letter]. It launched that fleet in late July 2026 and expected 20–25 second-generation driverless trucks by the end of September [P, Q2 2026 shareholder letter]; CNBC reported 20 on the road on 22 Sep 2026 [T]. It targets more than 200 by year-end 2026, which it says translates to a revenue run-rate of about \$80 M a year for its Transportation-as-a-Service business [P, Q2 2026 shareholder letter].
